## Why differentiate again? {#gac2-motion .gac-lesson}

<p class="gac-lead">For motion along a straight line, position is a function of time.</p>

<div class="gac2-rate-chain" role="group" aria-label="Differentiating position with respect to time gives velocity; differentiating velocity with respect to time gives acceleration">
<div class="gac2-rate"><h3>Position</h3><div data-math="s(t)"></div><p>Where is it?</p><small>metres</small></div>
<div class="gac2-rate-arrow" aria-hidden="true"><span data-math="\dfrac{d}{dt}"></span><span>→</span></div>
<div class="gac2-rate"><h3>Velocity</h3><div data-math="v(t)=s'(t)"></div><p>How is position changing?</p><small>metres per second</small></div>
<div class="gac2-rate-arrow" aria-hidden="true"><span data-math="\dfrac{d}{dt}"></span><span>→</span></div>
<div class="gac2-rate"><h3>Acceleration</h3><div data-math="a(t)=s''(t)"></div><p>How is velocity changing?</p><small>metres per second squared</small></div>
</div>

<p class="takeaway"><span data-math="\displaystyle a(t)=\frac{dv}{dt}=\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{ds}{dt}\right)=\frac{d^2s}{dt^2}"></span></p>

::: notes
Additional context, about 2 minutes. This is an actual mathematical relationship used in mechanics, rather than an invented numerical story. Restrict the interpretation to one-dimensional motion; s is position relative to a fixed origin, not total distance travelled. Velocity may be negative. Acceleration describes change in velocity, not necessarily an increase in speed.

Read both arrows as "differentiate with respect to time". The second derivative applies the same operation a second time. Units change from metres to metres per second to metres per second squared; the 2 in the derivative notation records the order of differentiation. Later in the lesson the independent variable returns to x.

NASA Glenn Research Center, Aircraft Translations, explains position, velocity and acceleration and their use in describing aircraft motion: https://www1.grc.nasa.gov/beginners-guide-to-aeronautics/aircraft-translations/ . No motion calculation or new motion formula needs to be memorised here.
:::
